vocab.title: Match each verb to its meaning
defs: to finally understand something after thinking about it
to organize or prepare something so it can start
to decide to do something later instead of now
to stop doing or having something for good
to finally do something you have wanted to do for a long time
to start a new activity or hobby
to say no to an offer or an invitation
to think of an idea, a plan or an answer

paras: For ten years, Carla Mendes said yes to everything. A panel at a conference, a new committee, a colleague who needed help with a presentation at nine at night. She was good at her job, and people knew it, so the requests never stopped. “I never turned anything down,” she says. “I thought that was what a good manager did.”

The change started with a small thing. She ran into an old colleague at an airport, and he asked her what she was reading. She could not remember the last book she had finished. She had put off her Spanish class for two years, and she had given up running without noticing. “I had a full calendar and an empty life,” she says.

So in January she came up with a rule. Every new request had to wait one day before she answered. If it was still a good idea the next day, she said yes. If not, she turned it down, politely. It took her a few weeks to figure out how to say no without apologizing, and she put a few difficult conversations off for too long. But she carried on.

By June, she had turned down eleven invitations and two projects. With the time she saved, she took up Spanish again, and she finally got round to writing a training guide her team had needed for years. “Nobody was angry,” she says. “Most people just asked somebody else. I had been saying yes to protect a reputation nobody was watching.”

She does not recommend saying no to everything. Her rule is about time, not about refusal. “The first answer is the fast one. The second answer, a day later, is the honest one. I just learned to wait for the second one.”

listenings.text: Every yes has a cost, and almost nobody counts it. When you say yes to a meeting, to a panel, to a favor, you are also saying no to something else. Usually it is something you never chose to give up: an evening, a piece of work that matters, sleep. I ask every new client to do one exercise. For one week, write down every request you agreed to, and how long each one took. Most people are shocked. They come back with twenty or thirty yeses, and two or three of them actually mattered. The others were just easier than saying no at that moment. So my advice is simple, and it is not to say no to everything. It is to stop answering immediately. When somebody asks you for something, say let me check and get back to you. That one sentence gives you a day to decide, and a day is usually enough to see whether the yes is worth it.

Here is a question learners ask me all the time. Why does English have two verbs for everything? Postpone and put off. Establish and set up. Decline and turn down. The answer is history. Most of the long, formal verbs came into English from Latin, through French, after the year one thousand and sixty-six. They became the language of law, government and business. The short ones, the phrasal verbs, come from the old Germanic part of English, the everyday words that people used at home and in the street. That is why, even today, they feel so different. A phrasal verb sounds like a conversation. A Latin verb sounds like a document. So my advice is practical. Use the formal verb in a written report, where it sounds precise. Use the phrasal verb when you are talking, where the formal one makes you sound like a document reading itself out loud.
